name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: An AI enablement audit in finance examines whether an organization's use of AI systems is fit for purpose, properly documented, and aligned with internal controls and external obligations. It covers model inventories, data feeds, decision thresholds, human oversight points, and the downstream accounting and reporting effects. The audit also checks that AI tools used in forecasting, credit scoring, fraud detection, or reconciliation are actually enabled rather than shadow IT. It is distinct from a pure technology review because it focuses on financial statement risk and operational resilience.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in finance examines whether an organization's use of AI systems is fit for purpose, properly documented, and aligned with internal controls and external obligations. It covers model inventories, data feeds, decision thresholds, human oversight points, and the downstream accounting and reporting effects. The audit also checks that AI tools used in forecasting, credit scoring, fraud detection, or reconciliation are actually enabled rather than shadow IT. It is distinct from a pure technology review because it focuses on financial statement risk and operational resilience.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same systems it reviews: the firm's data warehouses, model registries, identity and access management, and workflow logs. Auditors need read access to training data lineage, feature stores, version control for models, and the dashboards that business units use to monitor outputs. In many finance teams this means working across cloud data platforms, ERP modules, and vendor APIs that feed AI services. The infrastructure question is whether the audit trail exists and can be trusted, not whether the model is technically advanced.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by mapping each AI use case to a control objective, then testing evidence against that objective. Auditors sample model inputs and outputs, compare them to documented policies, and trace decisions back to source data. They interview model owners, review change logs, and run independent checks on fairness, accuracy, and drift where the data allows. The method is closer to internal audit and SOX-style control testing than to data science, with an emphasis on reproducibility and sign-off.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on who can change a model, what data it may use, and how its outputs affect people or capital. The audit asks whether consent, licensing, and retention rules are met for training and inference data, and whether model provenance is recorded from development through retirement. It also checks that risk limits, escalation paths, and human review are in place for high-impact decisions. Provenance failures, such as a model retrained on unapproved data, are treated as control deficiencies rather than technical bugs.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The audit is moving toward continuous assurance, where control evidence is collected automatically from model registries and data pipelines instead of once a year. Regulators and audit committees increasingly expect finance teams to show live lineage for AI systems and to explain model changes in plain language. As generative AI enters routine accounting tasks, the enablement audit will likely expand to cover prompt governance, retrieval sources, and the separation of AI-generated drafts from human-approved entries. The direction is less about checking boxes and more about proving that AI remains within the financial control environment.
